rationale: The conceptual point of the section depends on changing only the prior while holding the test characteristics fixed. A matched comparison makes that controlled contrast clearer than two isolated calculations.
subject: Comparison of 1% and 20% prevalence scenarios with identical test characteristics.
context: Place after the section's comparison to consolidate how changing the starting prevalence alters the composition of positive results and therefore the posterior probability.
reasoning_supported: Learners isolate the prior as the changing quantity and compare its effect on posterior probability while recognising that the evidence model remains constant.
canonical_discipline_note: Hold the 90% positive rate with the condition and 5% positive rate without the condition constant across both scenarios.
must_show: 1% prevalence leading to a posterior of about 15.4%
20% prevalence leading to a posterior of about 81.8%
90% positive rate among people with the condition in both scenarios
5% positive rate among people without the condition in both scenarios
A clear indication that prevalence is the quantity that changes
must_not_show: Different test characteristics between the two scenarios
An implication that the test becomes more accurate when prevalence rises
allowed_claims: The same test characteristics can yield different posterior probabilities when the prior changes.
The prior contributes to the interpretation of the evidence.
disallowed_claims: Higher prevalence makes the test itself more accurate.
source_basis: S5 controlled prevalence comparison, synthesis, and commissioned matched base-rate comparison.
caption_intent: Changing the prior from 1% to 20% changes the posterior even though the test characteristics remain fixed.
alt_text: Matched comparison showing identical 90% and 5% test rates with prevalence changing from 1% to 20%, producing posterior probabilities of about 15.4% and 81.8%.
detailed_description: Two parallel scenarios use populations of 10,000 and identical test characteristics. The first begins with 1% prevalence and ends with a posterior of about 15.4%. The second begins with 20% prevalence and ends with a posterior of about 81.8%. Shared annotations make clear that the test rates are held constant while prevalence changes.
